title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
authors: Tianle Liu, Gongbo Cheng, Chenggong Ni et al.
abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. title: Uniform Information Density-Based Preference Optimization
authors: Yongyuan Li, Yang Xu
abstract: To enable large language models to generate outputs that align with human preferences, optimization algorithms based on the comparison between chosen and rejected output pairs have been developed and been proven effective. Some recent endeavors have utilized certain linguistically-derived assumptions about the preference pairs to guide the design of more precise optimization directions. title: LLM-based User-Product Relevance Evaluation for Dynamic Product Advertising
authors: Wen Zhang, Xiao Bai, Hsiang-wei Chao et al.
abstract: Dynamic Product Advertising (DPA) retrieval systems are a core component of modern e-commerce advertising; however, their evaluation remains challenging. Conventional offline engagement metrics are limited by sparse, biased feedback, while online evaluation is costly and time-consuming. In this work, we propose a user--product relevance metric for offline evaluation of DPA retrieval systems. title: Scale, Drivers, and Limits of Representational Alignment Across Large Language Models
authors: Jialin Wu, Meenakshi Khosla
abstract: Comparing large language models can reveal shared representational structure and systematic differences between them. However, aggregate similarity measures can obscure how agreement varies across geometric scales and which linguistic properties support it. We introduce two complementary methods to resolve where models agree and what supports that agreement. title: Only What You've Signed up For: Secure Workflows with Constrained Diffusion Agents
authors: Michael Cardei, Anjun Hu, Chenrui Ma et al.
abstract: As agentic AI systems take on increasingly complex and consequential tasks, securing them against prompt injection becomes critical. Existing defenses often rely on detecting or reasoning about injected malicious instructions and can therefore remain vulnerable to adaptive attacks that optimize the injection itself. title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
authors: Defne Circi, Krystelle Lionti, Sarathkrishna Swaminathan et al.
abstract: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and

title: Swarm Telepathy: Prefill-Free KV-Cache Transfer Across Families
authors: Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem, Irene Tenison, Yang Zhang et al.
abstract: LLM multi-agent systems split work across agents that communicate through text. An agent summarizes its findings, another agent receives the text. This constrains communication to discrete tokens and costs redundant compute, limiting bandwidth and capabilities of multi-agent systems. Recent works demonstrate KV-cache transfer between LLMs but they either require the LLMs to be within the same family or cannot function across context, thus requiring the receiver to prefill text. title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
authors: Yuxuan Liu, Zhaochen Su, Hangyu Guo et al.
abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. title: Towards Merging-conditional Backdoor Unalignment against Large Language Models
authors: Yukun Chen, Yidou Chen, Yiming Li et al.
abstract: Model merging has become widely adopted for enhancing the task-specific performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) without additional training. While the specialized model from third-party platforms may undergo safety audits (e.g., backdoor detection), we reveal a novel and critical threat: One-sided Merging-Conditional Backdoor (OMCB). title: TagBO: LLM-Driven Task-Aware Graph Bayesian Optimization for Scientific Discovery
authors: Xinzhe Yuan, Zimu Zeng, Zhuo Chen et al.
abstract: Mixed-variable optimization in scientific discovery often requires exploring large combinatorial spaces under costly experimental evaluations, making sample?efficient Bayesian optimization (BO) essential. However, existing BO methods typ?ically rely on structural descriptors to define similarity among categorical variables, implicitly assuming that structural similarity reflects similarity in task performance. title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
authors: Yuqiu Deng, Muyun Jiang, Zongpeng Zhang et al.
abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. title: Verifiable Retrieval for Legal Reasoning through Structure-driven Knowledge Graph
authors: Ibrahim Siddig, Sviatoslav Tugeev, Munir Georges
abstract: Any automation within reliability-critical contexts such as medicine or law has to be transparent and verifiable. Despite their advantages, current LLM-based systems do not meet these requirements due to their inherent black-box nature. Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) attempts to ground the generative process in the relevant interpretable documents, thereby reducing the risk of AI 'hallucinations' and potentially enabling verification of the initial generation context. title: SmartSalesBench: A Resistance-Aware Multi-Turn Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Sales Agents
authors: P N Bhargav Teja, Velpula Lokesh Reddy, Madhu Basumata et al.
abstract: We present SmartSalesBench, the first multi-turn conversational benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate large language model (LLM) sales agents against psychologically grounded, resistant buyer personas. Existing task-oriented dialogue benchmarks assume cooperative users and measure task completion; SmartSalesBench inverts this assumption, placing agents against personas programmed to resist and challenge across conversations of up to twenty turns. title: Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
authors: Chenxu Zhang, Yaorui Shi, Wenlong Zhang et al.
abstract: Training long-horizon language model agents requires assigning credit to intermediate decisions from sparse terminal feedback. Within a finite group of sibling rollouts, useful action comparisons depend on their context, evidence for both alternatives, and how that evidence enters learning. We propose Matched-Context Group Policy Optimization (MCGPO), a procedure for constructing weighted action preferences from already collected trajectories. title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
authors: Ivan Moloshnikov, Dmitry Kunitsyn, Alexander Sboev et al.
abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. title: Humanize Olympiad Agents: A Multi-Session Workflow for Olympiad Problem Solving with Solve, Review, Wiki, Verify
authors: Zhengyang Zhang, Jing Xiong, Hongzhou Lin et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are rapidly improving on long-horizon scientific and olympiad tasks. Recent systems have produced a Lean-formalized resolution of the Navier--Stokes problem and autonomous solutions to four open questions in the Erdős Conjectures database. Yet neither system releases both its underlying model and complete inference stack. title: Proactive Agentic Orchestration
authors: Xueyang Feng, Chaozhuo Li, Xiaohe Bo et al.
abstract: Agentic orchestration delegates tasks to sub-agents with independent contexts, providing a key path to extending the effective execution horizon of large language model agents. However, existing orchestration methods face two limitations: in execution, current methods fix sub-agents' goals and harnesses at creation time, limiting their adaptability to dynamic real-world environments; in optimization, sparse and delayed feedback constrains effective learning of the orchestration policy. To addres

title: Agentic Large Language Models
authors: Max van Duijn, Michiel van der Meer, Aske Plaat et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? title: Rollout-Time Intervention: Unlocking Agentic Reinforcement Learning Beyond Policy Limits
authors: Chen Xi, Ding Ruixue, Wang Zhigaoyuan et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a key paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) agents, enabling stronger reasoning, planning, and tool-use in interactive environments. However, existing agent RL methods remain fundamentally constrained by an on-policy reasoning bottleneck: when tasks exceed the model's current capability boundary, effective trajectories become extremely sparse and training often collapses. title: Web$hell: A Unified Interface for Agentic Web Access
authors: Sunghwan Kim, Deogyong Kim, Sangam Lee et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming direct users of the open web. As they take on increasingly complex and information-intensive tasks, effective web access is becoming a core capability for agentic problem solving. Existing approaches have advanced agentic web access through different access models, including search-augmented agents, browser-based agents, and, more recently, filesystem-based agents. Nevertheless, as users expect agents to complete long-horizon, end-to-end tasks, they

title: PRIME: Pre-Retrieval Index Modeling Enhancement for Structured Document Retrieval-Real
authors: Cheuk Hei Chung, Li Liu
abstract: High-precision retrieval over external knowledge bases is essential for LLM agents to operate effectively. However, existing Information Retrieval (IR) research primarily optimizes query-side retrievers (e.g., ColBERT, BGE) and generators (e.g., Self-RAG, GraphRAG), while reducing corpus-side representation to chunking. title: Agent4Spec: An LLM-based Agentic System to Optimize API Specifications through Automated Validation and Market Analysis
authors: Yongjian Tang, Costel Moraru, Doruk Tuncel et al.
abstract: API specifications serve as critical documentation for modern software development, directly impacting integration efficiency and client code generation. While recent advancements have leveraged Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate initial specifications from source code, existing approaches treat this process as a one-time event - overlooking the needs for continuous validation, long-term maintenance, and market-driven evolution of these artifacts. title: Forgetting is Not Always Bad: A Neuro-Inspired Memory Repair Mechanism for Poisoned LLM Agents
authors: Lei Liu, Yunji Liang, Xiaowen Zhang et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are highly vulnerable to memory-poisoning attacks. Existing defenses primarily rely on external modules for either static memory isolation or continuous online auditing, resulting in low memory efficiency and high computational overhead. title: RoleWorld: Knowledge Transfer in World Modeling with Functional Role Abstractions
authors: Boyuan Xiao, Pu Wang, Ji Feng et al.
abstract: World models enable large language model (LLM) agents to anticipate action effects and make informed decisions. For generalization, it is desirable for such world models to transfer efficiently to new environments with similar interaction structure and underlying dynamics. Recent approaches encode world dynamics as symbolic rules or executable programs, whose compositional structure in principle affords transfer, but still organize such knowledge around environment-specific objects. title: DRYLAB-Bench: Benchmarking the Biosecurity Risk of Agentic LLM Mutation Design
authors: Yuzhen Wang, Chunxiao Li, Baichen Le et al.
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) acquire advanced biological design capabilities, they offer substantial research benefits but simultaneously introduce severe dual-use risks, such as engineering enhanced pathogens or drug-resistant bacteria. While biosecurity frameworks recognize these threats, the actual risk of LLMs executing dangerous biological modifications remains unquantified, particularly when augmented with specialized biological design tools (BDTs). Existing evaluations primarily assess

title: When Faster Decisions Do Not Make Better Agents: An Empirical Study of Jev in Agent Workflows
authors: Yuchen Ling, Shengcheng Yu, Zhenyu Chen et al.
abstract: AI agents depend on repeated decisions to accomplish tasks, with large language models (LLMs) commonly serving as their core decision makers. The recent emergence of Jev offers an opportunity to make these decisions faster and at lower cost. However, it remains unclear whether such local savings can be translated into efficient and reliable task completion. title: Travel Back To Move Forward: Retrospective Exploration and Evolving for Long Horizon Agents
authors: Ziang Ye, Wentao Shi, Lei Chen et al.
abstract: Large language model agents increasingly operate in long-horizon environments where early mistakes can trigger cascading failures and trap agents in dead-end trajectories. Agents must therefore be able to proactively recover from such states and turn their exploratory experience into guidance for subsequent decisions. title: Hindsight Structured Advice Distillation: Steering Executor Agents with Advisors Trained on Their Failures and Task Characteristics
authors: O. Ozan Koyluoglu
abstract: Language-model agents are used for specialized work such as financial research, healthcare and law. Such agents are often capable enough for a task but still miss its details. In finance, for example, these details include which filing reports a figure or how a company discloses a metric. Retraining the agent to learn these details is expensive, and often impossible when the agent is a closed or shared system. title: OccludeBench: Can VLMs Find What's Missing?
authors: Jasin Cekinmez, Addison J. Wu, Ryo Mitsuhashi et al.
abstract: How well can vision-language models (VLMs) reason about what is missing from an image? We study this question with OccludeBench, a manually curated benchmark for recovering fully occluded objects from the visual evidence that remains. OccludeBench distinguishes direct cases, where the hidden object must be recovered from a specific physical cue such as a shadow or reflection, from inferential cases, where it can be inferred from broader scene context. title: SpatialASM: Internalizing Active Mentalization for Spatial Reasoning
authors: Yuhong Liu, Shenxi Wu, Junyi Chi et al.
abstract: When solving complex spatial reasoning tasks, ordinary humans naturally revisit the scenes from task-relevant viewpoints and mentally reconstruct the spatial layouts from those viewpoints. But can Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) proactively think in the same way? title: Same Query, Different Answer: Run-to-Run Variance in Semantic Query Processing
authors: Oktie Hassanzadeh, Dharmashankar Subramanian
abstract: Semantic query engines ask a large language model (LLM) to judge individual rows, and benchmarks compare these engines on the quality of a few executions at temperature 0. We measure how much another execution changes. We re-execute the text and tabular workloads of SemBench, LRO-Bench, and UDA-Bench through their own harnesses, log every one of 1.2 million model calls, and reanalyze SemBench's published executions. title: Inject a Turn, Not a Token: Learning Where to Redirect LLM Reasoning for Self-Correction
authors: Jiwon Jeon, Myungsik Cho, Jeonghye Kim et al.
abstract: Large language models struggle to reliably identify and correct errors in their own reasoning. Unlike prior training-based approaches that fine-tune an LLM to generate revisions or feedback, we learn where to intervene in failed rollouts and determine how to redirect them. To choose where to intervene, we train a 130K-parameter MLP head on a frozen encoder using only final-answer correctness. title: MoPrO-SD: Modular Prompt Optimization for Stance Detection
authors: Meysam Sabbaghan, Nikesh Gyawali, Arman Zareian Jahromi et al.
abstract: Stance detection remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) due to implicit opinions, sarcasm, and context-dependent expressions of stance. Although automatic prompt optimization offers an alternative to fine-tuning without updating model parameters, existing structured approaches are not specifically designed around stance-label semantics and class-specific ambiguities. title: Test-Time Memory Construction
authors: Zijun Wang, Yifan Ji, Haidong Xin et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to answer questions over long interaction histories, where relevant evidence may be scattered across distant sessions. Existing memory systems typically construct and maintain sophisticated memory representations offline, before user queries are observed, incurring substantial overhead and limiting their ability to adapt memory construction to query-specific information needs. In this paper, we propose T$^2$Mem, a Test-Time Memory construction framework that

title: AdaC-GRPO: Towards Mastering Long-Horizon Visual Sudoku Puzzles via Adaptive Curriculum Learning
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Linli Yao et al.
abstract: While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. title: PreSTO: Predictive Subtree Prefetching for Fast LLM Power Sampling
authors: Nan Jiang, Panagiotis Theodoropoulos, Wei Deng
abstract: Power sampling improves large language model (LLM) reasoning at test time by sampling from a sharpened version of the base model's distribution. Its sampler, PowerMH, is slow because its Metropolis--Hastings (MH) updates are sequential: each accept/reject decision sets the state from which the next proposal is generated. title: Attention Sees, MLP Refuses: Tracing the Attention-to-MLP Safety Pathway in LLMs
authors: Zixuan Weng, Haoqi He, Weifei Jin et al.
abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. title: KV-Repurpose: A Testbed for Evaluating Non-Prefix KV-Cache Reuse
authors: Taiga Ikeda, Daisuke Miyashita, Jun Deguchi
abstract: KV-cache reuse in large language model serving is commonly limited to exact prompt prefixes, preventing reuse when the same retrieved document appears after different system prompts, conversation histories, or dynamic metadata. We present KV-Repurpose, an open-source, vLLM-based system for developing and evaluating segment-wise KV-cache reuse beyond exact prefixes. title: CliQ-RRG: Clinical-Knowledge Guided Disease-aware Visual-Textual Alignment for QA-Style Radiology Report Generation
authors: Chandravardhan Singh Raghaw, Shahid Shafi Dar, Arnav Nishith Sharma et al.
abstract: Radiology reports are essential for diagnostic reasoning and patient care, yet their manual preparation is time-consuming and cognitively demanding. Automatic radiology report generation (RRG) offers a scalable alternative, but existing models often produce lengthy, unstructured narratives that overlook diagnostic cues and multi-view information. title: What Should SFT Learn? Conditional Information Gain for Generalizable Post-Training
authors: Yuxuan Gu, Kequan Niu, Xiaocheng Feng et al.
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) remains a widely used approach for post-training large language models, because fixed demonstrations can directly introduce desired reasoning strategies and behavioral patterns. Yet forcing a model to imitate externally provided trajectories may also interfere with behaviors already supported by pretraining, limiting generalization beyond the training distribution. title: Learning More by Training Less: Uncertainty-Guided Progressive Contraction for Efficient Reasoning Post-Training
authors: Suorong Yang, Jiaxin Wang, Jiaming Su et al.
abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable advances in complex reasoning. However, scaling reasoning post-training with ever-larger corpora can substantially increase training cost without proportional performance gains. In this study, we therefore ask: how far can reasoning supervision be compressed without sacrificing capability? title: Collaborative Learning and Reasoning over Model Slices
authors: Yuheng Wang, Runde Yang, Zhuohan Bao et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel across diverse tasks, benefiting from knowledge priors, in-context reasoning, and test-time computation. Despite these strengths, single-model reasoning remains vulnerable to error propagation, as later steps depend on the model's earlier outputs, leaving reasoning blind spots difficult to independently reassess. title: Mind the Spatial Gap: A Benchmark for Geospatial Reasoning and Constrained Spatial Editing
authors: Zheng Ren, Yanning Wang, Ziheng Huang et al.
abstract: Understanding and manipulating spatial relations is fundamental to AI systems that reason about physical environments and construct grounded world models. However, existing evaluations of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for spatial reasoning rely predominantly on static question-answering (QA) over small-scale or synthetic scenes, rarely probing whether models can modify spatial configurations while satisfying explicit geometric constraints. title: Collaborative Theory of Mind: Learning to Self-Revise by Anticipating User Responses
authors: Fanzhi Zeng, Anubrata Das, Maytal Saar-Tsechansky et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong individual task performance, yet still struggle to collaborate with users over extended, multi-turn interactions, for example by attempting solutions before understanding the user's needs or by failing to revise mistaken assumptions after receiving feedback. title: UkrMeme: Multimodal Explainable Persuasion Detection in Ukrainian Memes
authors: Nazar Andrushko, Vera Schmitt, Veronika Solopova
abstract: Memes play a central role in modern online communication, especially in contexts of political conflict where visual and textual cues combine to convey persuasive messages. We study persuasive technique detection in Ukrainian memes using vision-language models (VLMs). title: AudioTETRIS: Token Elimination via Transitional Importance Signals for Efficient Audio LLMs
authors: Shreya Sajid, Anna Vettoruzzo, Joaquin Vanschoren
abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) achieve strong performance on speech-text tasks, but standard audio encoders produce hundreds of tokens for even short audio clips. Because self-attention scales quadratically in sequence length, this inflates inference-time compute substantially. Current training-free token compression methods prune or merge tokens based solely on coarse attention or feature similarity. title: S-Space: Exploring Spatial Workspace in Multimodal Language Models
authors: Zhiyuan Shi, Xiang Li, Xingzhuo Guo et al.
abstract: Multimodal language models (MLLMs) exhibit promising spatial reasoning capabilities, yet the internal mechanisms supporting them remain poorly understood. We uncover S-Space, a linear representation subspace in which object-token representations encode continuous coordinates along horizontal, vertical, and distance axes. title: Retrieval-Augmented Multimodal Language Model with Heterogeneous Evidence Integration for Clinical Prognosis
authors: Hamza Shafiq, Jialu Tang, Ting Dang et al.
abstract: Clinical prognosis requires integrating structured measurements, physiological waveforms, longitudinal history, and population context. We introduce PRISM (Population-Retrieved Inference for Structured Multimodal Prognosis), a multimodal language model that combines per-feature numerical tokenization, recency-weighted aggregation of longitudinal ECGs, and a dual-modality population memory bank. title: When MLLMs miss what humans read: diagnosing and learning to read squint text
authors: Chen Peng, Shan Huang, Jianbo Huang et al.
abstract: Multimodal LLMs can fail to read text embedded in an image's coarse structure (text a human recovers by squinting) and report that no text is present. We name this class Squint Text and study it as a recognition deficiency, motivated by cases from a production moderation pipeline. We introduce SquintBench, comprising 1076 production-derived moderation images, and SquintCtrl, a controlled synthetic suite for mechanism diagnosis. title: The Evidence Anchoring Boundary: Where Visual Interventions Matter and When They Help in Multimodal LLMs
authors: Qiji Zhou, Junyi Hu, Peiyu Wang et al.
abstract: Visual interventions provide a training-free way to reduce hallucinations in multimodal large language models. However, an intervention may have little leverage at some layers and may damage a correct answer even when it changes the output. We investigate where visual interventions retain leverage and when they improve predictions. title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
authors: Gangyi Li, LuYao Wang, Jingfu Sun et al.
abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. title: Not Just an Evaluation: A Case Study of Discourse Particle Sensitivity in Language Models
authors: William Sheffield, Jiahui Chen, Amy Zhang et al.
abstract: Discourse particles subtly shape the flow of discourse by reflecting conversational context and interlocutor attitudes, often leaving the truth-conditional meaning untouched. They are also often polyfunctional, with distinct senses which partially overlap with other particles; for example, the exclusive use of English "just" and "only" ("John only/just drinks water"). title: Not All Dimensions Are Equal: Outlier-Aware Attention Linearization with Grouped Quadratic Kernels
authors: Weiqi Sun, Qianyue Wu, Wenjia Wang et al.
abstract: Linearizing softmax attention offers a route to efficient Transformer inference, but preserving pretrained attention remains challenging. We identify an important source of approximation error overlooked by standard linearization methods: a small number of outlier dimensions contribute disproportionately to query-key dot products and account for a large fraction of the approximation error. title: Hide and Seek: HIDE Concepts to SEEK explanations for black box models
authors: Bhanu Tokas, Rahul Nair, Rockwell Jackson et al.
abstract: Interpreting machine learning model predictions is a central challenge, particularly for black-box vision models. Concept-based attribution methods interpret models using human-understandable concepts. Existing concept-based methods can only interpret classification and regression models. They require access to model weights or large concept-annotated datasets, and most methods cannot provide image-level attribution. title: Tracing and Taming Hallucinated Terms via Subsequence-Association Filtering and Breadth-Aware Selection for LLM Query Expansion
authors: Amit Kumar Jaiswal, Sagar Uprety, Prayag Tiwari
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now a standard source of query expansion terms but they hallucinate. They inject non existent entities and off-topic terms that add ranking noise and can hurt strong retrievers. title: What Do Audio-Language Judges of Generated Music Listen For? Four Probes with Controls from Expert Ratings
authors: Mateusz Modrzejewski, Tomasz Radzikowski
abstract: Open audio-language models are used as judges of generated music: given a clip and its text prompt, the model rates the clip, and the judge is validated by how well its ratings correlate with expert ratings. The correlation does not show what the judge responds to: the music, the text prompt, or the way the question is asked. title: SharP: Soft and Hard Prompt-Guided Augmentation with LLM for Low Resource Fake News Detection
authors: Ziyu Luo, Wei Li, Haoping Huang et al.
abstract: Fake news detection under low resource conditions is challenged by the scarcity of labeled data and the difficulty of capturing subtle deceptive patterns. In this work, we focus on low resource fake news detection, where only a small labeled set is available for training, while evaluation is performed under a fixed and unchanged test protocol. This setting is motivated by costly, ambiguous fact-checking and emerging topics and domains that are poorly covered by existing benchmarks. Existing data

title: VETR: Execution-Grounded Self-Improving Agent for Symbolic Graphics Reasoning
authors: Yingbo Ma, Kuangshi Ai, Gordon Dai et al.
abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. title: Evaluating LLM Creativity through Long-Tail Performance
authors: Yichen Wang, Tenghao Huang, Vishakh Padmakumar et al.
abstract: Creativity benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) vary widely in task and metric design. This raises the question of whether they capture a common notion of creativity. We propose that this shared target can be formalized as task-specific performance in the long tail of a reference input-output distribution, which describes how common input-output pairs are relative to a chosen source of text. title: MVGraph: Benchmarking LVLMs on Evidence Composition across Multi-View Visual Graph
authors: Yingjie Zhu, Han Cheng, Xuefeng Bai et al.
abstract: We introduce MVGraph, a benchmark for evaluating large vision-language models (LVLMs) on multi-graph reasoning where the evidence required by a query is distributed across multiple interrelated visual graph views. title: Surfing the Activation Wave: Analyzing the Information and Geometry of LLM Hidden States for Speculative Decoding
authors: Raghavv Goel, Sudhanshu Agrawal, Mukul Gagrani et al.
abstract: Decoder hidden states from different layers of large language models (LLMs) often encode complementary information. However, existing speculative decoding methods typically rely on a small set of target-model layers chosen using fixed, position-based heuristics. Selecting an optimal subset of layers is inherently a combinatorial problem, making exhaustive evaluation infeasible even for moderately deep models. In this work, we present a principled framework for multi-layer hidden-state selection

title: Neural networks are more modular than single neurons suggest
authors: Shreya Saha, Benjamin Bergen, Meenakshi Khosla
abstract: Neural networks routinely develop representations in which individual neurons contribute to multiple distinct functions, leading to the widespread view that such networks lack modular organization. title: Task Context Shapes Component Roles in Language Models
authors: Sovesh Mohapatra, Dani S Bassett
abstract: Large language models reuse the same attention heads across tasks, but identifying these shared heads does not explain what they do differently in each task. A natural source of inspiration is task-dependent interactions among shared brain regions, which motivate a network view of language-model computation. title: QTestBench: A Test Framework for Evaluating LLM-Generated Quantum Code
authors: Meriem Terki, Nouhaila Innan, Minghao Shao et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong results in classical code generation and are increasingly used to write the unit tests that safeguard that code. Whether they can do the same for quantum software is less clear, because quantum programs are probabilistic, depend on numerical tolerances, and are judged by domain-specific checkers, so a well-formed test can still disagree with the benchmark's verdict. title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
authors: Bastian Schäfer, Dominika Matus, Lennart Purucker et al.
abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. title: AMLworld-Compact: Importance-Weighted Downsampling for Cost-Effective LLM Evaluation and Error Diagnosis
authors: Natapong Nitarach, Phume Ngampornsukswadi, Pittawat Taveekitworachai et al.
abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on AMLworld's smallest test splits is costly because each of over a million targets requires a separate graph prompt. Sampling reduces this cost, but small balanced subsets change unweighted precision and F1. We introduce AMLworld-Compact, an evaluation set that retains every illicit test transaction and samples benign transactions from supervised-score strata. title: SWE-DeceptionBench: Benchmarking Deceptive Behaviors of LLMs Across the Software Development Lifecycle
authors: Xiting Liu, Lin Yang, Yitong Zhang et al.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used throughout the software development lifecycle. This growing reliance on LLMs raises concerns about their trustworthiness, with deception posing a particularly important risk. Deceptive behavior takes the form of misleading responses or assistance in fabricating, concealing, or distorting information. title: Towards the Roof of the World: NLP Progress in Tibetan Languages
authors: Xi Cao, Yijie Li, Yuan Sun et al.
abstract: Tibetan, spoken by some seven million people on and around the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, remains underrepresented in natural language processing (NLP). We present, to our knowledge, the first peer-reviewed systematic bibliometric survey of Tibetan NLP: 140 publications from 2004 to 2026 in the ACL Anthology and DBLP, annotated for venue type, research area, first-affiliation country, and resource release. title: Exploring Attention Sinks in Text-to-Image Transformers from Diffusion and Autoregressive Models
authors: Binglei Li, Mengping Yang, Zhiyu Tan et al.
abstract: Attention sinks are tokens or positions that consistently receive disproportionate attention mass, often beyond what their semantic content would suggest. Despite extensive study in large language models, their behavior and functional relevance in text-to-image (T2I) Transformers remain largely unexplored. title: Host-Aware Web Crawling for LLM Pretraining Data
authors: Malte Ostendorff
abstract: Web crawling is a major source of large language model (LLM) pretraining data, yet data-selection pipelines discard a large share of crawled pages. We investigate how a crawler should allocate its budget across and within hosts to collect more high-quality pretraining data. Combining document-level quality classifier scores, web-graph centrality metrics, and Common Crawl's per-host crawl coverage, we find that roughly half of the variation in classifier scores occurs between hosts. title: Tabular Foundation Models Are Effectively Shallow
authors: Irene Cannistraci, Julia E. Vogt
abstract: In-context-learning Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) are uniquely suited to scenarios with limited resources or privacy constraints, as they solve new tasks without additional training. However, their architecture consists of multiple transformer blocks, resulting in high computational and memory footprints. title: VIGOR: Verifiable Industrial Geometry Optimization and Repair in Scene Programs
authors: Fuqiang Wang, Zheng Guo, Xiaoming Wu et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate structured layouts and executable scene programs from natural-language instructions. However, executability does not imply engineering feasibility: an industrial scene program may execute successfully while its final state still violates coupled boundary, collision, clearance, aisle, or structural constraints. title: DP-MIND: Differentially private memory-guided Long context Inference
authors: Zhihao Liu, Yitian Cheng, Shuang Liu et al.
abstract: LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. title: Mitigating Capability Degradation in LLM Self-Improvement via Representation Geometry Regularization
authors: Jiaqi Tian, Ting Long
abstract: On-Policy Self-distillation is a self-improvement paradigm that enables large language models (LLMs) to improve their capabilities by leveraging the same model as both teacher and student under different conditioning contexts. title: X-AgentRed: Red-Teaming Personal Agents in Evolving Multi-Service Ecosystems
authors: Yeonsung Jung, Zhiyuan Wang, Zifan Wang et al.
abstract: Personal agents increasingly connect to services across the web and applications by using tools. As the effects of their actions accumulate and interact across services, unintended or harmful outcomes can arise when agents fulfill benign user requests. Proactively identifying these compositional failures requires systematically exploring diverse cross-service paths. Existing red-teaming methods often simply prompt LLMs to identify potentially harmful paths from task and environment descriptions

title: Rationally Linearized MLPs
authors: Arijit Sehanobish, Byeongchan Kim, Avinava Dubey et al.
abstract: We present Rationally Linearized Multilayer Perceptrons(RaLiMPs), a new approach to efficiently linearizing MLPs using low-degree rational approximations of standard activation functions. Inspired by polynomial-based MLP linearization, we show that rational approximations can provide accurate representations at substantially lower degree. title: Simulating Training Spikes of Deep Neural Networks by Layer-wise Random Feature Models
authors: Ran Tian, Courtney Paquette
abstract: Intermittent ``spikes'' in loss, during the pre-training of Large Language Models (LLMs), remains a mysterious phenomenon both theoretically and empirically. In this paper, we show that simple quadratic models with heavy-tailed, power-law distributed inputs can replicate these spikes. title: Humanize MLE Agents: Multi-Agent Session Alternation Beyond Single-Agent Limits
authors: Changye Li, Zijian Zhang, Muheng Li et al.
abstract: Existing LLM-based agent approaches for long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) often use context engineering, implemented through custom harnesses that manage tools, skills, and accumulated experience. However, we find that as single-session execution lengthens, the agent's reasoning intensity declines alongside slowing progress, summarized as long-horizon deceleration, and the benefits of these custom harnesses vanish as the underlying model improves, summarized as harness staleness. title: SWE-Critix: Post-Training Generalist Verifiers for Assessing Coding-Agent Trajectories
authors: Jiajun Hu, Chun Yong Chong
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly deployed for end-to-end software engineering tasks, where a readily available oracle evaluator that defines the success criteria is often absent. This motivates verifications for coding agents that can reliably judge and explain their behavior. However, verification is non-trivial as coding agents are increasingly capable of solving long-horizon software engineering tasks. title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
authors: Jaehyeon Park, Mingu Kang, Dongseok Lee et al.
abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. title: BoundaryEvo: Data-Model Co-Evolution at the Capability Boundary for Long-Chain Reasoning Distillation
authors: Jiaming Su, Suorong Yang, Xudong Li et al.
abstract: Distilling long-chain reasoning trajectories from large teacher models provides an effective way to improve the reasoning ability of small language models. However, existing methods typically select a fixed training set before distillation, overlooking that the usefulness of a reasoning example changes as the student evolves. title: Quality, Not Just Outcome: A Structural Scoring Framework for Selecting Coding-Agent Trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning
authors: Sida Li, Yuanxin Liu, Shicheng Li et al.
abstract: Open coding agents are commonly trained through supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories whose final patches pass the benchmark test suite. However, this outcome-level filtering criterion ignores process quality: trajectories that eventually succeed may still contain inefficient interaction patterns such as repetitive file inspection, unstable tool usage, or delayed modification behavior, all of which become part of the imitation target. title: CB-Orchestrator: Adaptive Workflow Optimization for LLM Agents via Contextual Bandits
authors: Jiahang Sun, Zhiwei Shang, Zhipiao Liu et al.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in tackling complex tasks through agentic workflows. However, manually designing these workflows is labor-intensive and lacks flexibility to adapt to diverse queries. While automated workflow optimization is a promising direction, existing methods often incur expensive API costs during training-phase feedback collection. title: Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization: Closing the State Distribution Gap in Long-Horizon LLM RL
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Weinan Dai, Yuyan Zhou et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a dominant paradigm for enhancing LLMs' reasoning capabilities. Yet long-horizon autoregressive rollouts introduce a fundamental limitation: local policy mismatch can compound into severe state distribution shift over trajectories. Existing LLM RL methods, such as GRPO and GSPO, control policy mismatch at the token or sequence level, but overlook this trajectory-induced shift, causing training instability and eventual collapse as the horizon grows. title: Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization: Unifying LLM RL Algorithms from the Perspective of Divergence
authors: Zhicheng Cai, Xinyuan Guo, Hanlin Wu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. title: Diffusion Precipitation Generation with Medium-range Weather Forecasting
authors: Guowen Li, Yang Liu, Mengxuan Chen et al.
abstract: Accurate daily precipitation forecasts are important for weather-sensitive decisions. Although recent Weather Foundation Models (WFMs) have achieved significant progress, they are trained on reanalysis data, which exhibit regional and intensity-dependent biases. title: GIST: Generator-state-Informed Supervision for Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Zhangyang Peng, Jingze Shi, Tongyi Zhang et al.
abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) based on prior-data fitted networks typically use sampled hard query labels, leaving avoidable sampling variability in pretraining. A key observation is that intermediate generator states can reveal label uncertainty beyond a sampled outcome. authors: Qingwen Lin, Boyan Xu, Shifeng Xie et al.
abstract: Non-autoregressive multi-step forecasting (NAF) enables time series foundation models to predict an entire future horizon in a single forward pass. Despite its strong sequence modeling capabilities, RWKV-7 exhibits long-horizon degradation in our NAF experiments. title: Temporal Evidence Forests for Long-Horizon Multi-Party Conversational Memory
authors: Junyou Guo, Chongyang Tao, Yan He et al.
abstract: Long-term memory has been widely adopted in LLM-based agents to support persistent interaction and personalized assistance. Long-term multi-party interactions, however, accumulate substantially more detailed information, with decisions repeatedly updated and states evolving across participants and interaction stages. title: ACED-Bench: Evaluating How LLM Agents Acquire and Act on Causal Evidence
authors: Yiwei Chen, Amila Weerasinghe, Siddharth Biswal et al.
abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as scientific assistants, yet we still lack reliable ways to evaluate whether they can investigate a system rather than merely answer a prompt. A useful evaluation must let agents choose experiments, interpret finite evidence, and make causal decisions, while keeping the environment coherent across repeated observations and interventions and preserving objective ground truth. title: Evaluating LLMs as Agentic Workflow Executors in Real-World Customer Support Skills
authors: Md Tahmid Rahman Laskar, Gundeep Singh, Xue-Yong Fu et al.
abstract: Enterprise customer-support agents increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) to execute bounded, tool-using workflows. We study this problem through the lens of Skill LLMs: specialized executors that operate within a selected skill context and must complete a narrow, stateful workflow under policy and tool constraints. title: Harness^2: Recursive Agent Harnessing for an Open World
authors: Ruiyao Xu, Yanfei Chen, Zhongying CuiZhu et al.
abstract: LLM agents' capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses. However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical challenges. title: Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
authors: Sahil Garg, Ruhi Gottumukkala, Vishal Agarwal et al.
abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store. We evaluate twenty-six models, nineteen open-weight and seven closed, under a common harness, scorer and panel of LLM judges.

authors: Hansi Yang, Linji Hao, Hongyan Hao et al.
abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. title: The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
authors: Xue Li, Hongqian Xia, Daniel Gomm et al.
abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. authors: Xiaofan Li, Fengchun Qiao, Xing Gao
abstract: In Model Context Protocol (MCP) systems, LLMs select tools from metadata rather than from their implementations. Names and descriptions summarize what a tool does, while the parameter schema specifies the fields a tool accepts and how they are organized. authors: Jialiang Sun, Kuldeep Meel
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance in mathematical and logical reasoning, yet they still suffer from the curse of complexity and struggle as problem difficulty increases with the number of constraint interactions and the size of the search space. authors: Georgios Batzolis, Georgios Kontos, Bruno Trentini et al.
abstract: We show that continuous bitstream diffusion (CoBit), originally developed for language modeling, provides a unified framework for joint and conditional multimodal generation using the same training and sampling protocol. authors: Laura Yao, Shixing Yu, Jie Peng et al.
abstract: Explaining a vision--language model (VLM) prediction requires tracing training-example influence to the multimodal evidence that mediates it, yet existing attribution methods largely operate only at the sample level. authors: Daniel J. Evans, J. P. Naiman, JooYoung Seo et al.
abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge.
